title: Best Microwaves 2026: Toshiba vs Panasonic vs Breville
description: Five microwaves compared on inverter vs standard power, even reheating and defrosting, sensor cooking, size, and price — from the budget Commercial Chef to the 3-in-1 Breville Combi Wave.
lede: The microwave's reputation for rubbery, unevenly-heated food is mostly a problem of cheap on/off power delivery, not the technology itself. The single upgrade that fixes cold-centre, overcooked-edge reheating is inverter power — and it's the spec that separates a microwave you tolerate from one that actually cooks evenly.

sections.heading: Top pick: Toshiba EM131A5C
paragraphs: The Toshiba EM131A5C is the best microwave for most kitchens because it delivers genuinely useful features — sensor cooking, even performance, and smart conveniences — at a mid-range price that represents excellent value. Its standout is sensor cooking: built-in humidity sensors detect when food is properly heated and automatically adjust the time and power, so you stop guessing and stop over- or under-cooking. It's a roomy mid-size unit (around 1.2 cubic feet, 1100 watts) that handles family-sized dishes, with one-touch presets, a mute option (you can silence the beeps), and an easy-to-read display.

It hits the sweet spot of capability and value: powerful enough to cook and reheat quickly, large enough for dinner plates and casserole dishes, and loaded with the conveniences (sensor reheat, popcorn and other presets, eco mode) that more expensive models offer, without the premium price. Toshiba has become one of the most recommended microwave brands precisely because units like this punch above their cost, with a stainless or black-stainless finish that looks good on a counter.

The honest caveats: it's a standard (not inverter) microwave, so for the smoothest, most even low-power cooking and defrosting the Panasonic inverter below edges it, and at 1.2 cubic feet it takes up real counter space. But for the best all-round balance of sensor cooking, capacity, performance, and price, the Toshiba EM131A5C is the default recommendation and the one that suits the most kitchens.

sections.heading: Best even cooking: Panasonic NN-SN966S Inverter
paragraphs: The Panasonic NN-SN966S is the pick for anyone who cares about even, gentle cooking and defrosting, because it uses inverter technology — and that's a genuine functional upgrade, not marketing. A standard microwave delivers, say, '50% power' by switching full power on and off repeatedly, which cooks the edges while the centre stays cold and overcooks delicate foods. An inverter delivers a steady, continuous stream of lower power, so 50% really means consistent half-power throughout — the result is dramatically more even reheating, gentle melting and softening without scorching, and defrosting that thaws evenly instead of cooking the edges while the middle stays frozen.

It's a powerful, large-capacity unit (around 1.2–2.2 cubic feet options, 1250 watts) with Panasonic's Genius sensor cooking that auto-adjusts time and power, plus a 'Turbo Defrost' that's noticeably faster and more even than standard defrost. The inverter design also makes the interior flatter and more spacious for its footprint. For someone who reheats a lot, cooks actual food (not just frozen meals) in the microwave, or hates rubbery, unevenly-heated leftovers, the inverter difference is the most worthwhile upgrade in microwaves.

The trade-offs: it's priced above basic microwaves, it's large, and the benefit is most noticeable to people who use the lower power levels and defrost often (if you only ever blast things on full power for two minutes, you'll notice the inverter advantage less). But for genuinely better, more even cooking and defrosting — the core complaint people have about microwaves — the Panasonic inverter is the standout.

sections.heading: The 3-in-1, the compact, and the budget picks: Breville Combi Wave, GE, Commercial Chef
paragraphs: The Breville Combi Wave 3-in-1 is the premium pick that replaces three appliances: it's a microwave, a convection oven, and an air fryer in one. Beyond microwaving, the convection function lets it bake and roast, and the built-in air-fry mode crisps food properly — so it can genuinely save counter space by combining a microwave with a small oven and air fryer. It uses inverter technology for even microwaving, has Breville's quality build and smart presets, and is the choice for someone with limited kitchen space who wants one capable appliance to do the work of several. It's expensive and the most complex option, but the versatility is real.

The GE JES1072SHSS is the compact, space-saving pick for small kitchens, dorms, offices, and anywhere counter space is tight. It's a small (around 0.7 cubic feet, 700 watts) no-frills microwave that does the fundamentals — reheating, defrosting, basic cooking — reliably in a footprint that fits where a full-size unit won't. It lacks sensor cooking, inverter power, and large capacity, so it's not for cooking family meals or fitting big dishes, but for a single person, a small space, or a secondary microwave, it's a dependable, affordable, appropriately-sized choice from a trusted brand.

The Commercial Chef Countertop is the rock-bottom budget pick — a basic, functional microwave at the lowest price for someone who just wants to reheat and defrost without spending much. It covers the essentials with simple controls and is available in various small-to-mid sizes. It has no sensor cooking, no inverter, and a more basic build, and the even-heating won't match the Panasonic, but for a rental, a first apartment, a budget kitchen, or anyone who treats the microwave purely as a reheating box, it does the job at minimal cost. It's the honest 'just need a microwave' choice.

sections.heading: How to choose: inverter vs standard, wattage, size, and sensor cooking
paragraphs: Understand inverter versus standard power, because it's the most meaningful quality difference. A standard microwave creates lower power levels by pulsing full power on and off, which causes uneven results — hot edges and cold centres when reheating, scorched spots when melting or softening, and defrosting that cooks the outside while the inside stays frozen. An inverter microwave (Panasonic, Breville Combi Wave) delivers steady, continuous lower power, so reduced power settings genuinely cook gently and evenly throughout, transforming reheating, defrosting, and delicate tasks like melting chocolate or softening butter. If you reheat leftovers often, cook real food in the microwave, or defrost regularly, the inverter upgrade is the one most worth paying for; if you only ever full-power-blast things, it matters less.

Match wattage and size to your cooking and your space. Wattage determines speed and cooking power: 700 watts (compact GE, budget units) is slower and fine for basic reheating in a small space, while 1000–1250 watts (Toshiba, Panasonic) cooks and reheats noticeably faster and handles more demanding tasks — for a main kitchen microwave, higher wattage is worth it. Capacity (cubic feet) determines what fits: compact ~0.7 cu ft units suit dorms and tight counters but won't hold a large dinner plate or casserole dish, while mid-to-large 1.2+ cu ft units (Toshiba, Panasonic) fit family-sized dishes. Measure your counter space and consider what dishes you actually microwave before choosing — bigger isn't automatically better if counter room is precious.

Weigh sensor cooking and extra functions for how you'll really use it. Sensor cooking (Toshiba, Panasonic) uses humidity or temperature sensors to detect when food is done and auto-adjust time and power — genuinely useful for foolproof reheating and cooking without guessing or overcooking. Multi-function units (Breville Combi Wave) that add convection baking and air frying are excellent if you want to save space by combining appliances, but add cost and complexity you don't need if you only microwave. Conveniences like a mute/silence option (surprisingly valued), one-touch presets, and an eco mode add daily polish. Decide whether you want a pure, even-heating microwave (Panasonic inverter), a feature-rich value all-rounder (Toshiba), a space-saving combo (Breville), a compact unit (GE), or a cheap basic box (Commercial Chef) — and buy for that, not the longest spec list.

faqs.q: What is an inverter microwave and is it worth it?
faqs.a: An inverter microwave is a genuine functional upgrade over a standard one, and it's worth it for anyone who does more than full-power blasting. The difference is how they deliver lower power levels. A standard microwave only has one power output — full — so to give you '50% power' it rapidly switches the full power on and off, which means food gets blasted then rests, blasted then rests, causing uneven results: hot edges and cold centres when reheating, scorching when melting or softening, and defrosting that cooks the outside while the inside stays frozen. An inverter microwave (like the Panasonic NN-SN966S and Breville Combi Wave) can actually deliver a steady, continuous stream of lower power, so 50% means a consistent half-power throughout — giving dramatically more even reheating, gentle melting and softening without scorching, and defrosting that thaws evenly. If you reheat leftovers regularly, cook real food in the microwave, or defrost often, the inverter is the most worthwhile microwave upgrade. If you genuinely only ever heat things on full power for a couple of minutes, you'll notice the benefit less and a good standard microwave like the Toshiba is fine.

faqs.q: How many watts should a microwave have?
faqs.a: It depends on whether it's your main kitchen microwave or a secondary/compact one. Wattage determines how quickly and powerfully a microwave cooks: higher wattage cooks faster and more effectively, and recipe times usually assume around 1000 watts. For a primary kitchen microwave, aim for 1000 watts or more (the Toshiba is 1100W, the Panasonic 1250W) — it reheats and cooks noticeably faster, handles more demanding tasks, and follows recipe timings accurately. Lower-wattage microwaves around 700 watts (like compact units and many budget models) are slower and you'll need to add time to cook things through, but they're perfectly adequate for basic reheating, drinks, and simple defrosting in a small space, dorm, or office, and they're cheaper and more compact. So: for a main microwave you cook with, choose 1000W+; for a secondary unit or a tight space where you mainly reheat, a 700W compact is fine and saves money and counter room. Just be aware that a low-wattage unit will feel slow if it's doing heavy daily duty.

faqs.q: What size microwave do I need and will it fit my counter?
faqs.a: Match the capacity to both what you cook and your available space, and measure before buying. Microwave capacity is given in cubic feet: compact units around 0.7 cu ft (like the GE JES1072SHSS) are small and space-saving — great for dorms, offices, small kitchens, and as a secondary microwave — but they often won't fit a large dinner plate or a casserole dish, which is a common frustration. Mid-size to large units around 1.2 cubic feet and up (like the Toshiba and Panasonic) comfortably fit family-sized plates and dishes and suit a main kitchen, at the cost of taking up significantly more counter space. The mistake people make in both directions is buying a compact unit and finding their dinner plate won't rotate inside it, or buying a large unit that dominates a small counter. So measure your available counter space (width, depth, and height, allowing for ventilation clearance and the door swing), and think about the largest dish you'll actually want to microwave, then choose the capacity that fits both. If counter space is tight but you cook real meals, that tension is exactly why combo units like the Breville (which replaces a microwave plus a small oven and air fryer) appeal.
